Veruela
veh-RWAY-lah
n. (the Aragonese Cistercian abbey of 1145, where Becquer wrote his Letters from my Cell in the emptied cloister)
Spanish Veruela, of uncertain origin, perhaps from a local water name.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Veruela under the Moncayo in Aragon was founded in 1145 by Pedro de Atarés and settled from Scala Dei in Gascony, one of the earliest Cistercian houses in the kingdom, with a walled precinct and a transitional church. It was suppressed in 1835. In the winter of 1863 and 1864 the poet Gustavo Adolfo Bécquer went there with his brother for his health and lived in the abandoned buildings, writing the Cartas desde mi celda, the Letters from my Cell, which are among the finest prose in Spanish and are the record of a man sitting in an emptied monastery thinking about mortality. Cistercians returned briefly in the twentieth century. The dictionary records Veruela for those letters, because they ask the question the building no longer answers. The psalmist states the measure of a man without softening it, “As for man, his days are as grass” (Psa 103:15), and Job puts the question itself and leaves it standing, “If a man die, shall he live again?” (Job 14:14). The expectation Scripture gives in place of a permanent cloister is frankly provisional, “For here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come” (Heb 13:14), and the posture it commends in the meantime is a waiting one, “It is good that a man should both hope and quietly wait for the salvation of the LORD” (Lam 3:26).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a cell as a small close apartment in a monastery; mortality as subjection to death; a precinct as a boundary; melancholy as a gloomy state of mind; and a hermitage as the habitation of a hermit.

expand to see more

CELL, n. A small or close apartment, as in a prison or monastery; a cave; a small religious house.

MORTALITY, n. Subjection to death or the necessity of dying; also, death, actual or frequency of death.

PRECINCT, n. The limit, bound or exterior line encompassing a place; a territorial district.

MELANCHOLY, n. A gloomy state of mind, often a gloomy state that is of some continuance.

HERMITAGE, n. The habitation of a hermit; a cell or a dwelling in a solitary place.

Key Scripture

Psa 103:15 — "As for man, his days are as grass: as a flower of the field, so he flourisheth."

Job 14:14 — "If a man die, shall he live again? all the days of my appointed time will I wait, till my change come."

Heb 13:14 — "For here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come."

Lam 3:26 — "It is good that a man should both hope and quietly wait for the salvation of the LORD."

Modern Corruption

Aragonese Cistercian abbey of 1145 where Becquer wrote the Letters from my Cell in the buildings after the monks had gone.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that an emptied monastery still puts the question it was built to answer. Becquer spent a winter writing in Veruela's abandoned cells, and the psalmist's measure of a man is as blunt as anything in those letters, “as a flower of the field, so he flourisheth” (Psa 103:15).

The live temptation is the melancholy itself, which can become a resting place where Scripture offers a direction. Job asks the question and does not answer it from inside himself, “all the days of my appointed time will I wait” (Job 14:14); the epistle makes every present dwelling provisional rather than tragic, “but we seek one to come” (Heb 13:14); and the posture commended in the interval has an object, “and quietly wait for the salvation of the LORD” (Lam 3:26).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew chatsir (H2682), grass; Hebrew chalaph (H2498), to change; Greek meno (G3306), to continue; Hebrew yachal (H3176), to hope.

expand to see more

Hebrew chatsir (H2682) — grass, herbage; “his days are as grass”, Psalm 103:15.

Hebrew tsits (H6731) — a blossom, a flower; “as a flower of the field”, Psalm 103:15.

Hebrew chalaph (H2498) — to change, to pass on; “till my change come”, Job 14:14.

Greek meno (G3306) — to abide, to remain, to continue; “here have we no continuing city”, Hebrews 13:14.

Hebrew yachal (H3176) — to hope, to wait patiently; “both hope and quietly wait”, Lamentations 3:26.

Usage

"“As for man, his days are as grass” (Psa 103:15) — as blunt as the Letters."

"“If a man die, shall he live again?” (Job 14:14) — the question left standing."

"“but we seek one to come” (Heb 13:14) — provisional, not tragic."
